notes.title: How the cuisine filters were policed
notes.body: Every food card names a specific dish — a cuisine label alone doesn’t qualify. Vietnamese, Chinese / Cantonese (dim sum), Sichuan, Thai (incl. Isan), Malaysian, Singaporean, wider Southeast Asian (Indonesian, Filipino, Burmese) and Persian each got a dedicated search led by Michelin (stars + Bib Gourmand), Eater, The Infatuation and NYT. Singaporean and Burmese are genuinely thin in NYC, so they are labelled as such rather than padded, and closed spots (Urban Hawker, Rangoon) were excluded. A Viral tag marks TikTok/Instagram-famous places whose virality is sourced to food media — not hype.

notes.title: Web-searched and fact-checked
notes.body: Every place is traceable to a credible source — Michelin, Eater, The Infatuation, NYT, Time Out, Atlas Obscura, Untapped New York, NYC Parks / NYC Tourism and official sites — recorded in data/sources.json (direct map/page fetches are blocked in the build environment, so sources were confirmed via search). Every coordinate is verified into data/geocodes.json and every place status-checked open.

places.w: 52-acre garden famed for its Japanese Hill-and-Pond Garden and springtime cherry-blossom esplanade.
Encyclopedic art museum on Eastern Parkway with Egyptian holdings and Judy Chicago's The Dinner Party.
526-acre Olmsted and Vaux park with the Long Meadow, a lake, and the Prospect Park Zoo.
Seaside amusement park home to the 1927 wooden Cyclone coaster; reopened for the 2026 season March 30.
478-acre 1838 garden cemetery and National Historic Landmark with monuments, ponds, and skyline views.
Restored 1922 carousel in a glass pavilion in Brooklyn Bridge Park beneath the Brooklyn Bridge.

places.ad: Washington St at Water St, Brooklyn, NY 11201
places.w: Cobblestoned Washington Street framing the Manhattan Bridge tower, one of NYC's most photographed views.
Cantilevered esplanade over the BQE with panoramic views of Lower Manhattan and the harbor.
Museum inside a decommissioned 1936 subway station with vintage subway cars on original track.
Family park built around the 1920 Wonder Wheel, a 150-foot NYC-landmark Ferris wheel with swinging cars.
1892 triumphal arch honoring Civil War veterans, anchoring Grand Army Plaza at Prospect Park's entrance.
Tiny Williamsburg community museum of NYC ephemera behind a bodega-style canopy; open Thursday-Sunday.
Five-acre Williamsburg waterfront park on the former Domino Sugar Refinery site with salvaged syrup tanks.
Open-air street-art gallery of rotating murals across warehouse walls around Troutman St and St. Nicholas Ave.
Historic-house museum of Weeksville, a free Black community founded in 1838, with restored Hunterfly Road Houses.
1.3-mile waterfront park across six DUMBO/Brooklyn Heights piers with lawns, kayaking and skyline views.
Landmarked 1927 wooden roller coaster at Luna Park, still rattling riders in its 99th season on the boardwalk.
Open-air weekend food market at Marsha P. Johnson State Park with 70+ vendors and Manhattan skyline views.
Historic boardwalk aquarium in Coney Island with sharks, sea otters and a coral reef Ocean Wonders hall.
Six-million-square-foot Sunset Park waterfront complex of food halls, makers, breweries and design studios.
Red Hook nonprofit cultural center fusing visual art, music and science in a restored 19th-century ironworks.
Crown Heights museum founded 1899, the world's first designed for children, with hands-on culture and nature exhibits.
Thirty hillside burial vaults from the 1850s inside Green-Wood Cemetery, opened only for guided tours and concerts.
Free three-floor exhibition center telling the shipbuilding and industrial history of the working Navy Yard.
New York City's oldest structure, a circa-1652 Dutch farmhouse in East Flatbush open for tours Fridays and Saturdays.
1849 Brooklyn Heights church, an abolitionist Underground Railroad stop where Lincoln and Beecher preached against slavery.
Free floating museum aboard the 1914 Lehigh Valley Barge No. 79, moored at Pier 44 in Red Hook.
One-dollar Coney Island USA museum of sideshow memorabilia, vintage arcade games and amusement-district history.
The largest metropolitan zoo in the US, 265 acres with 6,000+ animals, run by the Wildlife Conservation Society since 1899.
A 250-acre National Historic Landmark garden with the Victorian-era Enid A. Haupt Conservatory and 50 acres of old-growth forest.
Home of the New York Yankees since 2009, in the Concourse neighborhood; hosts baseball plus NYCFC soccer and concerts.
A 28-acre public garden and cultural center in Riverdale on a bluff above the Hudson with sweeping Palisades views.
The 1812 farmhouse where Poe spent his last years and wrote 'Annabel Lee'; now a museum run by the Bronx County Historical Society.
A 400-acre National Historic Landmark garden cemetery, resting place of Duke Ellington, Herman Melville and Miles Davis.
A 1.5-mile island in Long Island Sound with a New England fishing-village feel, seafood shacks, marinas and yacht clubs.
The 'Boulevard of Dreams,' a 1909 Champs-Elysees-inspired axis lined with one of the nation's densest concentrations of Art Deco buildings.
A Greek Revival stone mansion (c.1836-42) in Pelham Bay Park with period rooms and a formal terraced garden.
The oldest surviving building in the Bronx, a 1748 Georgian fieldstone house in Van Cortlandt Park.

places.n: The Bronx Museum of the Arts
places.w: A free contemporary-art museum on the Grand Concourse focused on 20th- and 21st-century work by artists of African, Asian and Latin American descent.

places.n: Hall of Fame for Great Americans
places.w: The first US hall of fame, a 630-foot open-air colonnade (1901, Stanford White) on the Bronx Community College campus with 98 bronze busts.
A 1924 limestone Italian Renaissance mansion built as a retirement home for the formerly wealthy; now a community arts and events space.
The Bronx's only public beach, a mile-long crescent in Pelham Bay Park built as a WPA project under Robert Moses in the 1930s, nicknamed the 'Bronx Riviera'.
NYC's third-largest park: 1,100+ acres of old forest, a freshwater lake, a 1748 stone manor and the nation's first public golf course.

places.ad: Bruckner Blvd & Westchester Ave, Bronx, NY 10461
places.w: The city's largest park at 2,700+ acres: salt marsh, hiking trails, a lagoon, a bird sanctuary and the crescent of Orchard Beach.

places.ad: University Ave & W 170th St, Bronx, NY 10452
places.w: NYC's oldest standing bridge (1848), a stone-arch former aqueduct reopened in 2015 as a pedestrian walkway across the Harlem River.
Free nonprofit photography and film gallery in Melrose mounting documentary exhibitions on social justice and the borough itself.
The apartment tower where DJ Kool Herc's August 1973 rec-room party gave birth to hip hop; state-recognized as the culture's birthplace.
A 1758 fieldstone farmhouse, the borough's second-oldest building, run as the Museum of Bronx History by the county historical society.
Riverfront greenway on the Bronx River where rusted 1940s concrete-batching towers were preserved as monumental industrial sculpture.
Weekend museum in an 1897 schoolhouse chronicling City Island's shipbuilding, oystering and America's Cup yacht-racing history.
Indoor market La Guardia built in 1940, packed with Italian butchers, cheesemongers, pasta stalls and hand-rolled cigars.

places.ad: E 161st St & Grand Concourse, Bronx, NY 10451
places.w: Free open-air food festival near Yankee Stadium gathering 50+ local vendors on select spring and fall dates; seasonal, check the schedule.
500-acre open-air sculpture park in the Hudson Highlands with monumental works by Calder, Serra, di Suvero, and a Maya Lin earthwork set across meadows and hills.
places.k: Hudson Valley (Orange County); ~1.5 hr drive, or Metro-North to Beacon plus shuttle. Seasonal (spring-fall), closed Tuesdays.

places.w: Dia's collection of 1960s-to-present minimal and land art in a former Nabisco box-printing factory, with vast daylit galleries of Richard Serra, Agnes Martin, and Dan Flavin.
places.k: Hudson Valley (Dutchess County); ~80 min on the Metro-North Hudson line to Beacon. Open Fri-Mon.

places.n: Walkway Over the Hudson State Historic Park
places.w: The world's longest elevated pedestrian bridge, a 1.28-mile former railroad span 212 feet above the Hudson linking Poughkeepsie and Highland.
places.k: Hudson Valley (Dutchess County); ~1.75 hr drive, or Metro-North to Poughkeepsie. Free; open daily 7am-sunset.

places.w: Six-story Rockefeller family mansion above the Hudson with Beaux-Arts gardens, a modern-sculpture collection, and a coach barn of classic cars and carriages.
places.k: Westchester (Sleepy Hollow); ~45 min drive. Guided tours only from the Philipsburg Manor visitor center. Tours are SUSPENDED for the 2026 season; confirm before visiting.

places.ad: 3006 Seven Lakes Drive, Bear Mountain, NY 10911
places.w: Hudson Highlands park with a summit auto road and Perkins Tower views toward the Manhattan skyline, a lakeside 1920s inn, a trailside zoo, and a merry-go-round.
places.k: Hudson Valley (Rockland/Orange counties); ~1 hr drive. Open year-round.

places.w: Well-preserved 19th-century riverfront village of antique shops and cafes across from Storm King, a gateway to Breakneck Ridge and Hudson Highlands hiking.
places.k: Hudson Valley (Putnam County); ~80 min on the Metro-North Hudson line, walkable straight from the station.

places.ad: 2107 New South Post Road, West Point, NY 10996
places.w: The nation's oldest continuously operating Army post and academy above the Hudson; public bus tours visit Trophy Point, the Cadet Chapel, and Battle Monument.
places.k: Hudson Valley (Orange County); ~1.5 hr drive. Access to the post is by guided bus tour only; bring government ID for the required background check.

places.w: Restored 18th-century Dutch-colonial milling and trading site with a working water mill, telling the story of the 23 enslaved Africans who ran it.
places.k: Westchester (Sleepy Hollow); ~45 min drive. Timed tours May-early November, Wed-Sun.

places.ad: 200 Morris Pesin Drive, Jersey City, NJ 07305
places.w: Waterfront NJ park facing the Statue of Liberty and Ellis Island, with the restored 1889 Central Railroad terminal, a 2-mile promenade, and ferries to the monuments.
places.k: New Jersey (Jersey City); ~25 min via PATH plus a short walk, or a quick drive. Open daily 6am-10pm.

places.w: 42-acre sculpture park and museum on former state fairgrounds, dotted with Seward Johnson's life-size bronzes set among gardens, ponds, and roaming peacocks.
places.k: New Jersey (Mercer County); ~1.5 hr drive, or NJ Transit to Hamilton. Closed Tuesdays.

places.w: Ivy League campus of Collegiate Gothic quadrangles anchored by 1756 Nassau Hall, once the U.S. capitol, with a free open-air Putnam sculpture collection.
places.k: New Jersey (Mercer County); ~1.5 hr by NJ Transit to Princeton Junction plus the Dinky shuttle. Free student-led campus tours.

places.w: Herzog & de Meuron-designed museum of American art in the Hamptons, strong in East End painters like Fairfield Porter and the region's postwar artists.
places.k: Long Island (Hamptons/Water Mill); ~2.5 hr drive, or LIRR to Southampton. Closed Tue-Wed.

places.ad: 71 Old Westbury Road, Old Westbury, NY 11568
places.w: Gold Coast estate of the Phipps family with a 1906 Charles II-style mansion and 200 acres of formal English gardens, ponds, and tree-lined allees.
places.k: Long Island (Nassau Gold Coast); ~45 min drive. Closed Tuesdays; grounds are seasonal, roughly April-December.

places.w: Robert Moses's 1929 Atlantic beach with 6.5 miles of sand, an Art Deco bathhouse and water tower, a long boardwalk, and a summer amphitheater.
places.k: Long Island (Nassau County); ~1 hr drive, or LIRR to Freeport/Wantagh plus a beach-bus shuttle. Busiest on summer weekends.

places.w: 168-foot black-and-white striped 1858 lighthouse on the barrier-island seashore, with a keepers' museum and a tower climb over the dunes and ocean.
places.k: Long Island (Fire Island); ~1.5 hr drive via the Robert Moses Causeway to Field 5, then a half-mile boardwalk. Seasonal; tower climbs weather-permitting.

places.w: New York's oldest lighthouse, authorized under George Washington and lit in 1796, at the easternmost tip of Long Island, with a museum and a tower climb.
places.k: Long Island (East End); ~3 hr drive or LIRR Montauk line, the farthest of these trips. Seasonal, roughly spring-fall.

places.w: Long Island wine-country estate near the Hamptons known for its dry rose and sparkling wines, with a year-round tasting room among the vines.
places.k: Long Island (East End/Sagaponack); ~2.5 hr drive, or LIRR to Bridgehampton plus a short ride. Tasting room open daily; reservations advised.

places.w: Encyclopedic art museum on Museum Mile with over 1.5 million works spanning 5,000 years, from Egyptian temples to European masters.
places.k: Pay-what-you-wish only for NY State residents; others pay a fixed admission. Closed Wednesdays.

places.w: 843-acre landscaped park by Olmsted and Vaux running from 59th to 110th Street, with Bethesda Terrace, the Ramble, and the Reservoir loop.
1931 Art Deco skyscraper with 86th and 102nd floor observatories offering 360-degree views across the city and beyond.
places.k: Timed tickets recommended; sunset slots sell out. Open late, past 11pm.

places.w: Open-air observation deck atop Rockefeller Center with an unobstructed head-on view of the Empire State Building and Central Park.
places.k: Entrance is on West 50th Street between Fifth and Sixth Avenues.

places.ad: Gansevoort Street & Washington Street, New York, NY 10014
places.w: 1.45-mile elevated park built on a former freight rail viaduct, running through Chelsea past gardens, art installations, and city views.
places.k: Southern entrance at Gansevoort St has elevator access. Free.

places.w: 1913 Beaux-Arts rail terminal with a celestial-mural ceiling over the Main Concourse and the acoustic Whispering Gallery by the Oyster Bar ramp.
places.k: Stand in opposite corners of the tiled archway to hear a whisper across the vault.

places.n: New York Public Library, Stephen A. Schwarzman Building
places.w: 1911 Beaux-Arts main branch guarded by the marble lions Patience and Fortitude, home to the vast third-floor Rose Main Reading Room.
places.k: Free entry; Rose Reading Room open Monday to Saturday.

places.ad: 99 Margaret Corbin Drive, New York, NY 10040
places.w: The Met's branch for medieval European art in Fort Tryon Park, built from parts of five French cloisters and home to the Unicorn Tapestries.
places.k: Far uptown in Washington Heights; admission is included with a Met ticket.

places.w: Greenwich Village square anchored by the Washington Arch and a central fountain, a longtime hub for street performers, chess, and NYU life.
places.k: Free; liveliest on warm weekend afternoons.

places.w: Henry Clay Frick's Gilded Age mansion showing Old Master paintings by Vermeer, Rembrandt, and Bellini; reopened April 2025 after a major renovation.
places.k: The mansion's second floor is now open to the public for the first time.

places.w: J.P. Morgan's 1906 private library in Murray Hill, with a three-tier tapestry-hung study and holdings from Gutenberg Bibles to literary manuscripts.
places.k: Closed Mondays; the historic library rooms are the highlight.

places.w: Restored 19th-century tenement telling immigrant stories through recreated apartments; entry is only by guided tour from the visitor center.
places.k: Tours must be booked; the museum interior is not open for free walk-ins.

places.w: Hidden one-acre park perched 40 feet above the Financial District, with a lawn, boardwalk, and East River views over the Brooklyn Bridge.
places.k: Reach it via an easy-to-miss escalator set back from Water Street.

places.w: Free Washington Heights museum with the finest collection of Spanish art outside Spain, including Goya, El Greco, and Sorolla's Vision of Spain murals.
places.k: Free timed ticket required as of January 2026.

places.ad: 555 Edgecombe Avenue, Apt 3F, New York, NY 10032
places.w: Free living-room jazz concert held every Sunday since 1993 in a Sugar Hill apartment, run by pianist Marjorie Eliot and family.
places.k: Sundays at 3pm; doors around 2:30pm. Free, donations welcome; arrive early for a seat.

places.ad: City Hall Station, New York, NY 10007
places.w: Ornate 1904 station with Guastavino-tiled vaults and skylights, closed to service since 1945; NY Transit Museum runs occasional member tours.
places.k: No regular access; you can glimpse it by staying on a downtown 6 train past the Brooklyn Bridge stop as it loops.

places.w: Twin reflecting pools sit in the footprints of the fallen towers; the museum below preserves the slurry wall and artifacts.

places.n: National Museum of the American Indian
places.w: Free Smithsonian collection of Native art housed inside the Beaux-Arts Alexander Hamilton U.S. Custom House.
Maya Lin-designed galleries tracing 160+ years of Chinese American history on the edge of Chinatown.
Tiny Battery Park City gallery devoted to the vertical city, with mirrored floors and ceilings echoing height. Free admission.
Site where Washington took the first presidential oath and the first Congress met; a Greek Revival landmark on Wall Street.
Gothic Revival church anchoring the head of Wall Street; Alexander Hamilton is buried in its churchyard.
Manhattan's oldest church in continuous use (1766); served as a relief station after 9/11, which happened across the street.
Sacred site marking a colonial-era cemetery of free and enslaved Africans, rediscovered during 1991 construction.
The only 19th-century family home in Manhattan preserved intact inside and out, furnishings and all.
The 1913 'Cathedral of Commerce' with a jaw-dropping mosaic-and-gargoyle lobby, viewable only on booked tours.
Free 25-minute round-trip harbor ride passing the Statue of Liberty and lower Manhattan's skyline.

places.ad: Broadway at Bowling Green, New York NY 10004
places.w: Arturo Di Modica's 7,000-pound bronze bull, an unsanctioned 1989 drop that became the icon of the Financial District.
Kristen Visbal's bronze girl now stands defiantly facing the New York Stock Exchange.
Whimsical Nolita sculpture garden saved from demolition in 2025 after a celebrity-backed community fight.
Colonial tavern where Washington bade farewell to his officers in 1783; museum upstairs, working tavern below.
Restored 1887 Eldridge Street Synagogue with a stunning stained-glass rose window by Kiki Smith.
Chinatown's largest Buddhist temple, home to a 16-foot golden Buddha, tucked beside the Manhattan Bridge.
Chinatown's social heart, where elders play xiangqi and mahjong and tai chi groups gather each morning.
A sharp-bending Chinatown lane once nicknamed the 'Bloody Angle,' now lined with murals and old shops.
Cobblestoned 17th-century lane, pedestrianized and packed with bar tables under string lights come evening.
A transplanted Irish fieldstone cottage and hillside in Battery Park City memorializing the Great Famine.
Walter De Maria's 1977 interior sculpture: a SoHo loft filled with 280,000 pounds of earth, free to visit.
Another De Maria installation: 500 polished brass rods laid in perfect rows across a SoHo gallery floor.
Santiago Calatrava's soaring white rib-cage transit hall, a winged marble concourse over the PATH station.

places.ad: Pier 55 at W 13th St, New York NY 10014
places.w: Free floating park on tulip-shaped concrete pots over the Hudson, with lawns, overlooks and an amphitheater.
Six floors of modern and contemporary art holding Van Gogh's Starry Night, Monet's Water Lilies, and a landmark design and film collection.
The 1932 Art Deco showplace inside Rockefeller Center, home of the Rockettes and the largest indoor theater of its era.
A 22-acre Art Deco complex with the golden Prometheus fountain, seasonal ice rink, and the Channel Gardens promenade.
A Neo-Gothic Roman Catholic cathedral of white marble on Fifth Avenue, its twin spires rising 330 feet opposite Rockefeller Center.
The 1930 Art Deco skyscraper with a stainless-steel sunburst crown, long a candidate for the city's most beautiful tower.
A formal green behind the main library with a carousel, free lawn games, a winter rink and holiday market, and cafe kiosks.
A block-long food hall in the former Nabisco Oreo factory, packed with vendors, tacos, seafood, and specialty shops.
Renzo Piano's tiered Meatpacking building with terraces over the Hudson, showing American art from the Whitney's deep 20th-century collection.
Daniel Burnham's 1902 triangular terracotta tower wedged where Broadway crosses Fifth Avenue; a defining view (exterior only, under residential conversion).
The West Village site of the 1969 uprising, the first U.S. national monument to LGBTQ history, with Christopher Park and an NPS visitor center.
The only NYC museum devoted solely to fashion, with a research-grade costume collection and free rotating exhibitions.

places.ad: Madison Ave & E 23rd St, New York, NY 10010
places.w: A leafy Flatiron square with rotating public art, dog runs, and the original Shake Shack kiosk under the trees.

places.ad: Union Square W & E 17th St, New York, NY 10003
places.w: The city's flagship farmers market since 1976, drawing regional growers and top chefs four days a week to Union Square.
A gated cobblestone lane of former 19th-century carriage houses just north of Washington Square, once home to Edward Hopper.
James Renwick Jr.'s 1846 French Gothic Revival masterpiece and National Historic Landmark where Broadway bends at 10th Street.
The Western Hemisphere's highest outdoor sky deck, a triangular platform jutting 80 feet out at the 100th floor with a glass floor.
Frank Lloyd Wright's white spiral ramp on Museum Mile, a modern-art collection you view by descending one continuous coil.
Intimate Gilded-Age mansion devoted to German and Austrian art, home to Klimt's gold 'Woman in Gold' portrait of Adele Bloch-Bauer.
The Smithsonian's design museum inside Andrew Carnegie's mansion, where an interactive pen lets you draw and save objects.
Warburg mansion holding 30,000 objects of Jewish art and history, from ancient Judaica to modern painting and rotating shows.

places.n: Museum of the City of New York
places.w: The city's own biography told through photographs, film and artifacts, including the sweeping 'Timescapes' history film.
Founded in East Harlem in 1969, the city's leading museum of Puerto Rican, Caribbean and Latin American art and culture.

places.ad: 200 Central Park West, New York NY 10024
places.w: The dinosaur halls, blue-whale model and Rose Center planetarium anchor one of the world's great natural-history collections.

places.ad: 170 Central Park West, New York NY 10024
places.w: The city's oldest museum, holding Tiffany lamps, all of Audubon's watercolors and a vast library of Americana across from the park.

places.n: Cathedral of St. John the Divine
places.w: Still-unfinished Gothic behemoth in Morningside Heights, one of the largest church buildings on earth, with a resident peacock garden.

places.ad: W 122nd St & Riverside Dr, New York NY 10027
places.w: Grant's Tomb, the granite mausoleum of Ulysses S. Grant and his wife, is the largest tomb in North America overlooking the Hudson.
Harlem's landmark stage where Amateur Night launched Ella Fitzgerald, James Brown and countless others since 1934.
The premier museum of artists of African descent, reopened November 2025 in a new David Adjaye-designed seven-floor building.
Alexander Hamilton's only home, a 1802 Federal-style country house moved to St. Nicholas Park and restored by the Park Service.
Manhattan's oldest surviving house, a 1765 mansion that served as Washington's Revolutionary War headquarters in Washington Heights.

places.ad: St. Nicholas Ave & W 155th St, New York NY 10031
places.w: The elevated Harlem enclave where W.E.B. Du Bois, Duke Ellington and Thurgood Marshall lived among grand rowhouses and Art Deco flats.

places.ad: Fort Washington Park, W 178th St, New York NY 10033
places.w: Jeffrey's Hook Light, the 1880 cast-iron lighthouse dwarfed beneath the George Washington Bridge and saved by a children's book.

places.ad: Riverside Dr to Broadway, New York NY 10040
places.w: Olmsted-designed clifftop park with the Heather Garden's terraced plantings and sweeping Hudson and Palisades views.

places.ad: Central Park, Terrace Dr at 72nd St, New York NY 10024
places.w: Central Park's grand ceremonial heart, its 'Angel of the Waters' fountain framed by an arcade of tiled ceilings above the Lake.

places.ad: Central Park, mid-park at 74th St, New York NY 10024
places.w: The graceful cast-iron span arcing over the Lake, Central Park's most photographed bridge and a fixture of countless films.

places.ad: Central Park, mid-park at 79th St, New York NY 10024
places.w: Calvert Vaux's Victorian folly perched on Vista Rock, a working weather station with the park's highest lookout.

places.ad: Central Park, Fifth Ave at E 105th St, New York NY 10029
places.w: Central Park's only formal garden, six acres of Italian, French and English planting entered through the Vanderbilt Gate.

places.ad: Central Park, mid-park 73rd-79th St, New York NY 10024
places.w: A deliberately wild 38-acre woodland of winding paths and a stream, prime warbler-migration birding in the heart of the park.

places.ad: Central Park, W 72nd St, New York NY 10023
places.w: The tear-shaped memorial garden to John Lennon opposite the Dakota, centered on the black-and-white 'Imagine' mosaic.

places.ad: Tramway Plaza, 2nd Ave & E 59th St, New York NY 10044
places.w: The aerial commuter cable car that glides beside the Queensboro Bridge, giving a four-minute skyline ride over the East River.

places.ad: 900 Southpoint Park, Roosevelt Island, New York NY 10044
places.w: The ivy-clad Gothic Revival shell of an 1856 smallpox hospital, the only ruin with official NYC landmark status.

places.ad: 14 N Moore St, New York, NY 10013
places.w: This active FDNY firehouse is the exterior of the Ghostbusters' HQ in the 1984 film and its sequels.
The comic-book address of Doctor Strange's Sanctum Sanctorum; the corner tenement is a real Village pilgrimage spot.

places.ad: 55 Central Park West, New York, NY 10023
places.w: Dana Barrett's apartment tower and the rooftop temple of Gozer in the original Ghostbusters; exteriors shot here.
The West Village corner building used for the exterior of Monica's apartment on Friends for all ten seasons.
The brownstone stoop that stood in for Carrie's apartment on Sex and the City from season three on.
Kevin McCallister's grand hotel in Home Alone 2: Lost in New York; still an operating landmark hotel.
The real skyscraper the filmmakers digitally topped to create Stark/Avengers Tower in the MCU films.

places.n: Men in Black HQ (Battery Vent Building)
places.w: The Brooklyn-Battery Tunnel ventilation building used as the MiB Headquarters exterior in all three films.
The Art Deco tower and its giant lobby globe served as the Daily Planet in the 1978 Superman film.

places.ad: 10 St. Luke's Place, New York, NY 10014
places.w: The Village brownstone used for exterior shots of the Huxtable home on The Cosby Show.
The Flemish Revival Harlem townhouse Wes Anderson rented as the Tenenbaum family home.

places.ad: 1 Wall Street Court, New York, NY 10005
places.w: The flatiron-shaped Beaver Building is the exterior of the assassins' Continental Hotel in the John Wick films.
Nintendo's two-story US flagship store with playable games, exclusive merch, and a museum of consoles.
The legendary toy store, home to a walk-on floor piano recalling Tom Hanks's dance in the movie Big.
LEGO's Rockefeller Center flagship, packed with NYC-themed brick builds and a Statue of Liberty model.
The jeweler Holly Golightly gazes into in Breakfast at Tiffany's; the store displays her film dress.

places.ad: W 167th St Step Street at Shakespeare Ave, Bronx, NY 10452

Nature center inside 635-acre Alley Pond Park, with boardwalk trails through tidal wetland and forest home to 300-plus wildlife species and a live-animal room.

21st-floor rooftop atop Hotel 50 Bowery with two open terraces giving 360-degree views over both the Manhattan and Brooklyn skylines
18th-floor 'urban amusement park' atop Moxy Times Square with a carousel, mini-golf and topiary gardens overlooking Midtown
26th-floor jewel-box lounge atop the historic Beekman Tower with 1920s Deco glamour and a terrace over the East River and Chrysler Building
Penthouse disco and rooftop atop The Standard, High Line in the Meatpacking District, complete with a plunge pool and Hudson River sunsets
José Andrés' 50th-floor sky lounge atop The Ritz-Carlton NoMad with mirrored ceilings and a 270-degree wraparound view of Midtown
Rooftop atop 1 Hotel Brooklyn Bridge with waterfront views straight across to the Manhattan skyline and the Brooklyn Bridge
Danny Meyer's restaurant perched 60 floors above Lower Manhattan with floor-to-ceiling views spanning the harbor and Downtown skyline
Two-Michelin-star dining room with floor-to-ceiling windows overlooking MoMA's sculpture garden in the heart of Midtown
Michelin-starred waterfront room under the Brooklyn Bridge with window tables framing the Lower Manhattan skyline across the East River
9th-floor restaurant atop the Museum of Arts and Design at Columbus Circle with panoramic views straight over Central Park
65th-floor bar at Rockefeller Center, the highest outdoor terrace in NYC, with 30-mile views past the Empire State Building

places.ad: 205 East Houston Street, New York, NY 10002
places.w: Cash-and-ticket Lower East Side deli open since 1888, serving 15,000 lbs of pastrami a week under old neon and salami-hanging signs.
Greenwich Village slice institution since 1975, turning out thin, foldable New York-style plain slices from a stand-up counter until the early hours.
Chinatown counter for Xi'an-style hand-pulled biang biang noodles and cumin lamb, grown from a Flushing basement stall into a beloved local chain.

places.ad: 179 East Houston Street, New York, NY 10002
places.w: Family-run appetizing shop since 1914, slicing smoked salmon, whitefish, and sable behind the counter of a landmark Lower East Side storefront.
Chelsea Market taco stand griddling adobada pork shaved from a trompo onto hand-pressed tortillas; standing-room only and near-constant lines.
1885 Garment District chophouse famous for its mammoth mutton chop, dry-aged steaks, and ceilings hung with thousands of clay churchwarden pipes.
Original Upper West Side basement bakery known for its thick, gooey-centered six-ounce chocolate chip walnut cookies baked to order.

places.ad: 328 Malcolm X Boulevard, New York, NY 10027
places.w: Harlem soul food landmark founded by Sylvia Woods in 1962, serving fried chicken, braised oxtails, and cornbread with weekend gospel brunch.
Michelin-starred ground-floor restaurant in an Art Deco tower; the golden pork katsu is the must-order.
Daniel Rose's Michelin-starred French room; unapologetically classic dishes in an airy candlelit space.
Chinatown's oldest dim sum parlor (1920) on a curved lane; the OG egg roll and shrimp dumplings are staples.
The Chinatown institution that put xiao long bao on the NYC map; order the crab-and-pork soup dumplings.
Michelin Bib Gourmand for made-to-order dim sum; the green snow pea leaf dumplings are the signature.
Michelin Bib Gourmand revival of the restaurant that popularized cold sesame noodles in NYC decades ago.
Late-night Cantonese standby famed for salt-baked seafood and window-hung roast duck.
Cash-only counter turning out gloriously cheap plates of char siu roast pork over rice; expect a line.
Chef Sam Yoo's diner under the Manhattan Bridge reimagining classics; the honey butter pancakes are a hit.
Basement Chinatown-American mainstay open since 1938, roast pork lo mein at all hours.
Chinatown stalwart carving crisp-skinned Peking duck tableside for wrapping in pancakes.
Billed as America's first pizzeria (1905); the coal-oven clam pie is the one to get.
The cult Nolita slice window; the curled-cup spicy spring pepperoni square draws constant lines.
Nolita red-sauce favorite; the thin-crust tie-dye pie swirls vodka sauce with pesto.
Scarr Pimentel's house-milled-flour slice shop on the LES, a wood-paneled throwback with a modern crust.
Keith McNally's bustling SoHo brasserie; steak frites and the raw bar under a zinc-and-mirror room.
LES brunch institution whose fluffy blueberry pancakes with maple butter built its reputation.
Little Italy pasticceria since 1892; shell-crisp cannoli filled to order and classic sfogliatelle.
Family Italian latteria since 1925 pulling fresh mozzarella to order alongside aged cheeses and cured meats.
The oldest bialy bakery in the U.S. (1936), hand-rolling onion-centered bialys and bagels on the LES.

places.ad: 137 E Houston St, New York NY 10002
places.w: Selling old-world baked potato knishes on Houston Street since 1910; a living LES relic.
No-reservations Greek taverna at the Chinatown-LES seam; flaming saganaki and grilled octopus.
Iberian-leaning seafood spot on Canal from the Hart's team; tinned fish, razor clams and vinho verde.
Michelin-starred Korean steakhouse mashing up KBBQ and an American chophouse, grilling dry-aged USDA Prime tableside.
Jody Williams and Rita Sodi's beloved rustic West Village gastroteca known for market vegetables and handmade pastas.
Danny Meyer's Michelin-starred seasonal-American institution; the front tavern room is walk-in and serves its famous burger.
Family-run Ukrainian diner in Little Ukraine since 1954, open late for pierogi, borscht, and potato pancakes.
Coal-oven pizzeria since 1915 serving whole pies only, no slices, from an 850-degree brick oven in the West Village.
Two-story Koreatown mainstay built around bubbling stone bowls of soft-tofu stew with banchan and cast-iron rice.
The first U.S. outpost of the Japanese chain, its rich pork-bone broth a benchmark for the city's ramen boom.
Brooks Headley's Bib Gourmand vegetarian burger counter turned sit-down diner, with cult veggie burgers and gelato.
Chef Hoyoung Kim's Michelin-starred Korean fine-dining room offering an approachable, grill-forward tasting near Flatiron.
A tiny Michelin-starred Gramercy tapas bar, Costa Brava-inspired, with adventurous plates and a wall of sherry.
Udon specialist on Curry Row where the chef hand-cuts thick, chewy noodles for hot and cold bowls plus chawanmushi.
An intimate East Village natural-wine bar with 250-plus bottles, orange-wine depth, and vegetable-driven counter cooking.
Eyal Shani's Israeli street-food stall inside Chelsea Market stuffing charred pita with cauliflower, lamb, and steak.
The self-styled 'Sturgeon King' since 1908, a UWS appetizing counter where scrambled eggs come folded with silky smoked sturgeon.

places.ad: 10 Lincoln Center Plaza, New York NY 10023
places.w: Kwame Onwuachi's Afro-Caribbean showpiece at Lincoln Center, where day-marinated braised oxtail and curry-goat patties draw long waits.
Marcus Samuelsson's lively Lenox Avenue dining room serving modern Harlem comfort food like fried yardbird and mac & greens.
Harlem soul-food institution whose menu names dishes for local figures; 'The Rev. Al Sharpton' pairs fried chicken with waffles.
Melba Wilson's Harlem comfort-food spot whose chicken and eggnog waffles beat Bobby Flay on a televised 'Throwdown'.
A Little Senegal mainstay serving Senegal's national dish, thieboudienne, plus lamb maffe in big communal portions.
Rustic smokehouse under the Riverside Drive viaduct, slow-smoking dry-rubbed St. Louis ribs since 2004 with blues on the side.
Washington Heights Dominican classic since 1987, famous for the garlicky spit-roasted chicken turning in its front window.
The famously impossible-to-book East Harlem Italian-American room, open since 1896, where the lemon chicken is legend.
East Harlem coal-oven pizzeria since 1933, said to have pioneered the pizza-by-the-slice walk-up counter still working today.
Viennese coffeehouse inside the Neue Galerie, serving Sachertorte and apple strudel beneath period paneling on Museum Mile.
Green-checkered Upper East Side pub since 1972 turning out a benchmark bacon cheeseburger with crisp cottage fries.
Upper West Side Southern comfort spot piling fried chicken on housemade biscuits alongside its namesake jarred pickles.
The Morningside Heights diner whose exterior stood in as Monk's on 'Seinfeld' and inspired Suzanne Vega's 'Tom's Diner'.
The 24-hour Upper West Side hot-dog stand at 72nd Street, famous for its griddled dogs and papaya-drink Recession Special.
The whimsical Upper East Side cafe where the John Cusack rom-com Serendipity is set and filmed.
The Midtown Irish bar whose back-wall mural inspired MacLaren's Pub on How I Met Your Mother.
The gleaming Art Deco Chelsea diner featured in Woody Allen's Manhattan and Men in Black II.
Perennially packed, no-reservations Astoria taverna considered among the city's best Greek seafood; expect a wait for the charred octopus.
Michelin-recommended Flushing institution famous for delicate, broth-filled Shanghai soup dumplings pleated to order.
The brick-and-mortar home of Maria Cano, the legendary Jackson Heights street vendor, serving sweet grilled corn arepas.
Fiery, regional Thai cooking in Elmhurst that draws citywide crowds for its panang duck, crispy pork and drunken noodles.
Tiny cash-only Flushing counter beloved for its No. 6, a dozen tender pork wontons swimming in roasted-chili oil.
Refined Chiapas-inspired Mexican in Long Island City, a former Michelin-starred spot known for cochinita pibil and mole de Piaxtla.
A hidden Tibetan counter tucked behind a cell-phone shop, an open secret for hand-pleated momos and thukpa noodle soup.
All-vegetarian South Indian canteen in the basement of the Ganesh Temple, prized for crisp dosas, idli and sambar at bargain prices.
The landmark that put Woodside Thai food on the map: fiery, no-compromise cooking, famous for its crackling fried watercress salad and jungle curries, plus a garden patio.
Corona institution since 1944 slinging dozens of hand-made Italian ices from a corner window; the classic lemon, packed with real rind, is the reason for the line.

places.ad: 18-24 College Point Blvd, College Point, NY 11356
places.w: Beloved off-the-beaten-path Sichuan kitchen worth the trek to College Point for numbing dan dan noodles, cumin lamb, and fish with pickled chili.
One of the few NYC spots specializing in fierce, garlic-and-chili Hunan cooking: Chairman Mao's red-braised pork, steamed fish head with chopped chili, cumin lamb.
Murray Hill Flushing Korean standby for bubbling soondubu jjigae (soft-tofu stew) cracked with a raw egg, alongside tabletop barbecue and generous banchan.
Multi-time Momo Crawl champion serving Nepali home cooking; the signature jhol momo drops dumplings into a spicy sesame-tomato broth. Chicken or beef fillings.
Tibetan momo counter under the 7 train, named for the Amdo region, hand-folding pillowy steamed beef dumplings deep into the night for the Himalayan diaspora.
The old-guard anchor of Little India, open since 1980, known for its charred tandoori mixed grill, goat curry, dosas, and a bustling weekend lunch buffet.
Roosevelt Avenue rotisserie beacon turning out crackling-skinned Colombian charcoal chicken with arepas, rice, and fries under bright, festive murals.
Old-school Astoria Greek taverna where the draw is simple whole fish and charred grilled octopus dressed in olive oil and vinegar, with a sidewalk garden in summer.
Tiny Steinway Street Egyptian counter where chef Ali cooks a menu-less feast to order: smoky grilled lamb chops, stuffed vegetables, ox tongue, and more.
Family-run Balkan pita house since 1997 rolling flaky coiled burek stuffed with meat, cheese, spinach, or potato, plus cevapi and thick drinkable yogurt.
Kosher Bukharian grill in Rego Park's Central Asian corridor: skewers of lamb, sweetbreads, and lamb testicle, plus the namesake fried chebureki turnovers.
Longtime Woodside Filipino grill billing 'the best BBQ in town': sweet-savory pork skewers, crispy pata, sisig, and kamayan feasts served on banana leaves.
Small, deeply spicy Elmhurst Thai favorite in the heart of Little Thailand, drawing crowds for pounded green papaya salad, larb, and crispy pork with basil.
Corona's cult Italian deli, aka Mama's, famed for its house mozzarella and the overstuffed Mama's Special hero; a neighborhood ritual near the ballfields.
Time-capsule Forest Hills soda fountain running since the 1920s, scooping house-made ice cream and hot fudge sundaes topped with real whipped cream at a marble counter.
Warm family-run Sunnyside spot, one of the city's only Paraguayan kitchens, serving crisp milanesa, vori vori dumpling soup, chipa, and grilled meats.
Seasonal beach-shack taqueria inside the Rockaway Beach Surf Club, famous for crispy Baja-style fish tacos eaten at picnic tables steps from the sand.
Bib Gourmand trattoria near the St. George ferry where a rotating cast of grandmothers cook regional Italian and 'Nonnas of the World' menus that change nightly.

places.ad: 524 Port Richmond Avenue, Staten Island, NY 10302
places.w: Blue-collar Port Richmond tavern serving thin, crackly-crust pizza since 1937 under the motto 'In crust we trust'; the plain cheese and garlic-onion white pies are the classics.
Family pizzeria running since 1960, famous for a paper-thin cracker crust and its vodka-sauce pie topped with fresh mozzarella and basil.
Cash-only Dongan Hills neighborhood tavern open since 1940, prized for a thin-crust white clam pie and old-school bar-pizza atmosphere.
Elaborately decorated Stapleton restaurant, among the first Sri Lankan spots in NYC, known for its weekend all-you-can-eat buffet of curries served on banana leaves.
Tiny, cash-only Tompkinsville storefront in 'Little Sri Lanka' cooking homestyle rice-and-curry and string hoppers from a steam-table counter since the late 1990s.

places.ad: 501 Port Richmond Avenue, Staten Island, NY 10302
places.w: The original 1928 Port Richmond stand, a summer institution serving scores of Italian-ice flavors plus cream-ice and ice-cream combinations from a walk-up window.

places.ad: 750 Port Richmond Ave, Staten Island, NY 10302
places.w: A Port Richmond institution long rated among the North Shore's best pizzerias, its thin-crust pies once featured on Bobby Flay's Throwdown.
A Bulls Head Sri Lankan kitchen from the family behind the old San Rasa, chopping griddled kottu roti and ladling fiery curries in the island's Sri Lankan corridor.

places.ad: 4254 Arthur Kill Rd, Staten Island, NY 10309
places.w: A tavern operating on this Charleston site since 1855, serving sauerbraten, schnitzel and steins of German beer in a carved-wood old-world dining room and biergarten.
A classic Italian bakery on Hylan Boulevard baking its own bread on premises, prized for savory lard bread studded with prosciutto and pecorino alongside pastries and sandwiches.

places.ad: 461 Port Richmond Ave, Staten Island, NY 10302
places.w: A Mexican restaurant and bakery anchoring Port Richmond's Little Mexico, open daily for tacos, guisados and pan dulce baked in-house.
A St. George spot near the ferry cooking West African plates of jollof rice, stews and soups, a foothold of the island's Liberian and African community.
